etymology: Webster 1828 prints NEXT as adjective (nearest in place, time, degree, rank, or relation) and as adverb (at the time or turn immediately succeeding). This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: nearest in order, and the turn that follows. Companion pages already treat time, order, and sabbath.
biblical_def:
Next is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. Nearest in place, time, rank, or relation. Next is what has nothing intervening. John writes, The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him. Order is not a vibe. Days follow days. The Lamb stands in history, not in a feed.

2. The turn immediately succeeding. As an adverb, next names the soonest following turn. On the next Sabbath almost the whole city came together to hear the word of God. The dictionary therefore keeps next from becoming a brand of restlessness. God orders the hours. A man does not author the calendar by craving the following thing.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: NEXT, adjective — nearest in place; nearest in time; nearest in degree, quality, rank, right or relation. NEXT, adverb — at the time or turn nearest or immediately succeeding.
webster_full: NEXT, adjective
1. Nearest in place; that has no object intervening between it and some other; immediately preceding, or preceding in order. We say, the next person before or after another.
2. Nearest in time; as the next day or hour; the next day before or after Easter.
3. Nearest in degree, quality, rank, right or relation; as, one man is next to another in excellence; one is next in kindred; one is next in rank or dignity.
NEXT, adverb At the time or turn nearest or immediately succeeding. It is not material who follows next.
scriptures: John 1:29
The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!
Acts 13:44
On the next Sabbath almost the whole city came together to hear the word of God.
corruption_summary: Next is corrupted when the following thing is crowned as meaning, when 'what's next' replaces the present obedience, and when Sabbath order is treated as a queue to skip.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the infinite scroll. Webster still knew next as nearest in a real order. The age catechizes men to live for the next hit, the next drop, the next version of themselves. John 1:29 is The next day — a dated hour in which the Lamb is seen, not a brand of novelty.

The second corruption is FOMO as discipleship. Acts 13:44 is the next Sabbath, the city gathered to hear the word of God. Hustle calls waiting a waste. The church that cannot keep a Sabbath cannot tell time.
The third corruption is succession as self-promotion. 'I am next' becomes a throne claim. Scripture's next is assigned nearness, not a campaign slogan.

Do not call restlessness a calling, and do not call order a bottleneck.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints PLEASE as verb transitive (to excite agreeable sensation; to satisfy; to prefer) and as verb intransitive (to like; to choose; as ceremony, to condescend). Latin placere. This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: to gratify or content, and to become the object of God's approbation. Companion pages already treat faith, flesh, and son.
biblical_def:
Please is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. To gratify, satisfy, or content. To please is to excite agreeable sensation, or to satisfy a wish. Men please the taste, the mind, a neighbor, a crowd. That is real. It is not yet worship.

2. To be approved by God. Webster says to please God is to love His character and law and perform His will, so as to become the object of His approbation. Paul cuts the boast: those who are in the flesh cannot please God. Without faith it is impossible to please Him. The dictionary therefore keeps please from becoming a people-pleasing gospel. God is pleased in His Son. Man is not saved by being agreeable.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: PLEASE, verb transitive — to excite agreeable sensations; to satisfy; to prefer. To please God is to love His character and law and perform His will. PLEASE, verb intransitive — to like; to choose; as ceremony, to condescend. PLEASE expresses less gratification than delight.
webster_full: PLEASE, verb transitive s as z. [Latin placere, placeo.]
1. To excite agreeable sensations or emotions in; to gratify; as, to please the taste; to please the mind.
2. To satisfy; to content.
3. To prefer; to have satisfaction in; to like; to choose.
To please God, is to love his character and law and perform his will, so as to become the object of his approbation.
They that are in the flesh cannot please God. Romans 8:8.
PLEASE, verb intransitive s as z. To like; to choose; to prefer.
1. To condescend; to comply; to be pleased; a word of ceremony.
PLEASE expresses less gratification than delight.
scriptures: Romans 8:8
So then, those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
Hebrews 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please Him, for he who comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him.
corruption_summary: Please is corrupted when self-pleasing is baptized as authenticity, when people-pleasing is recast as love, and when 'please God' is treated as a mood He owes the flesh.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is 'do what pleases you.' Webster still knew please as gratification under judgment. The age catechizes children to treat desire as a sacrament. Romans 8:8 is not wellness copy. Those in the flesh cannot please God.

The second corruption is the agreeable gospel. Love is recast as never disappointing the room. Hebrews 11:6 ties pleasing God to faith that He is, and that He rewards those who seek Him — not to charm, platform, or conflict-avoidance.
The third corruption is flipping the verb. God is asked to please us. Scripture's order is the reverse: we are to please Him, and we cannot do it in the flesh.

usage: Do not ask the flesh to please God; it cannot (Romans 8:8).
Come to God by faith, or you are only managing impressions (Hebrews 11:6).
Do not call crowd-approval worship, and do not call self-pleasing freedom.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints QUIET as adjective (still; unmolested; peaceable; calm), as noun (rest; tranquility; peace), and as verb (to still; to calm; to allay). Latin quietus / quies. This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: rest that is not agitated, and the meek spirit God calls precious. Companion pages already treat peace, rest, and meekness.
biblical_def:
Quiet is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. Still; at rest; not turbulent. Quiet is being in a state of rest, free from alarm, not exciting disorder. In Asa's days the land was quiet ten years. That is civil repose under providence, not emptied mind.

2. The meek and quiet spirit; a quiet life. Peter names the ornament of a gentle and quiet spirit, precious in the sight of God. Paul commands the church to aspire to lead a quiet life, mind its own business, and work with its own hands. The dictionary therefore keeps quiet from becoming a spa word or a gag order. God quiets. A man may also be told to be quiet when he ought to speak.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: QUIET, adjective — still; free from alarm; peaceable; calm. QUIET, noun — rest; tranquility; peace; security. QUIET, verb transitive — to stop motion; to calm; to allay.
webster_full: QUI'ET, adjective [Latin quietus.]
1. Still; being in a state of rest; now moving.
2. Still; free from alarm or disturbance; unmolested; as a quiet life.
3. Peaceable; not turbulent; not giving offense; not exciting controversy, disorder or trouble; mild; meek; contented. The ornament of a meek and quiet spirit.
4. Calm; not agitated by wind; as a quiet sea or atmosphere.
QUI'ET, noun [Latin quies.]
1. Rest; repose; stillness; the state of a thing not in motion.
2. Tranquility; freedom from disturbance or alarm; civil or political repose.
3. Peace; security.
QUI'ET, verb transitive
1. To stop motion; to still; to reduce to a state of rest.
2. To calm; to appease; to pacify; to lull; to tranquilize.
3. To allay; to suppress; as, to quiet pain or grief.
scriptures: 1 Peter 3:4
rather let it be the hidden person of the heart, with the incorruptible beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious in the sight of God.
1 Thessalonians 4:11
that you also aspire to lead a quiet life, to mind your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you,
corruption_summary: Quiet is corrupted when a meek spirit is recast as silenced compliance, when a quiet life is mocked as smallness, and when 'quiet' is sold as a nervous-system product with no God in it.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is wellness stillness. 1 Peter 3:4 is a quiet spirit precious in God's sight — not a breathing app. The age sells quiet as a nervous-system hack. Peter sells hidden character under God.
The second corruption is platform as virtue. 1 Thessalonians 4:11 is a quiet life, your own business, your own hands. Influence culture calls that failure. Paul calls it a command.

The third corruption is quiet as gag. Abusers and institutions tell the wounded to be quiet so the brand can rest. Biblical quiet is not a cover for sin. It is peaceable meekness, not a muzzle on truth.

usage: Seek the quiet spirit God calls precious, not the silence a brand requires (1 Peter 3:4).
Aspire to a quiet life and work with your hands (1 Thessalonians 4:11).
Do not call meekness cowardice, and do not call a muzzle peace.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints REFUSE as verb (to deny a request; to decline to accept; to reject) with s as z, and as a separate noun/adjective (worthless leftover; waste matter) with s as s. The stress moves. This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: the holy No, and what is thrown aside as worthless. Companion pages already treat obey, cornerstone, and pride.
biblical_def:
Refuse is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. To deny, decline, or reject. To refuse is to decline to do or grant what is asked, or to decline to accept what is offered. Edom refused Israel passage. The people refused to obey Samuel. Wisdom says, I have called and you refused. Refusal can be righteousness or rebellion. The verb does not baptize the will.

2. What is rejected as worthless. As noun and adjective, refuse is waste matter, left as unworthy of reception. That sense is not the same act as saying no. The dictionary therefore keeps refuse from becoming either a trash aesthetic or a slogan for authenticity. God may refuse. Man may refuse God. Those are not the same sentence.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: REFUSE, verb — to deny a request, demand, or command; to decline to accept; to reject. REFUSE, adjective/noun — rejected; worthless; waste matter. Webster notes that refuse expresses rejection more strongly than decline.
webster_full: REFU'SE, verb transitive s as z.
1. To deny a request, demand, invitation or command; to decline to do or grant what is solicited, claimed or commanded.
Thus Edom refused to give Israel passage through his border. Numbers 20:21.
2. To decline to accept what is offered; as, to refuse an office; to refuse an offer.
3. To reject; as, to refuse instruction or reproof.
The stone which the builders refused is become the head of the corner. Psalms 118:22.
Note — refuse expresses rejection more strongly than decline.
REFU'SE, verb intransitive s as z. To decline to accept; not to comply.
REF'USE, adjective Literally, refused; rejected; hence, worthless; of no value; left as unworthy of reception.
REF'USE, noun That which is refused or rejected as useless; waste matter.
scriptures: Numbers 20:21
Thus Edom refused to give Israel passage through his territory; so Israel turned away from him.
1 Samuel 8:19
Nevertheless the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel; and they said, No, but we will have a king over us
corruption_summary: Refuse is corrupted when a holy No is recast as toxicity, when refusing God is branded as authenticity, and when people are talked about as refuse.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is 'never refuse yourself.' Webster still knew refuse as a real denial. The age treats every boundary as cruelty and every appetite as a right. Numbers 20:21 is Edom's refusal — a national no with a history. Not every no is trauma.

The second corruption is refusing God as coming-of-age. 1 Samuel 8:19 is the people refusing Samuel so they may have a king. Therapy talk that names obedience 'self-betrayal' is that sentence with better lighting.
The third corruption is the noun as contempt. Calling image-bearers refuse is not edgy. It is a category error. Waste matter is not a people-group.

Do not refuse the voice God sent in order to crown your own king (1 Samuel 8:19).
Do not call appetite authenticity, and do not call a person waste.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints WRONG as adjective (wrung, twisted from the straight; not physically or morally right), as noun (injury; trespass; private or public), as adverb (amiss), and as verb (to injure; to treat with injustice). This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: what is not right, and the injury done. Companion pages already treat justice, sin, and judgment.
biblical_def:
Wrong is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. Not right; twisted from the line God drew. Wrong is what is not fit, not just, not according to truth. Webster's picture is physical first: wrung, twisted from a straight line. Then moral: that which deviates from the line of rectitude prescribed by God.

2. Injury done; to injure. As a noun, wrong is a trespass, private or public. As a verb, to wrong is to treat with injustice or to impute evil unjustly. The landowner says, Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Paul says the one who does wrong will be repaid, and there is no partiality. The dictionary therefore keeps wrong from becoming a feeling. God names the line. A wound is not the same thing as a verdict.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: WRONG, adjective — wrung, twisted from the straight; not physically or morally right; erroneous. WRONG, noun — injury; trespass; private or public. WRONG, adverb — amiss. WRONG, verb — to injure; to treat with injustice; to impute evil unjustly.
webster_full: WRONG, adjective Literally wrung, twisted or turned from a straight line or even surface. Hence,
1. Not physically right; not fit or suitable; as the wrong side of a garment.
2. Not morally right; that deviates from the line of rectitude prescribed by God; not just or equitable; not right or proper; not legal; erroneous.
3. Erroneous; not according to truth; as a wrong statement.
WRONG, noun Whatever deviates from moral rectitude; any injury done to another; a trespass; a violation of right. Wrongs are private or public.
Friend, I do thee no wrong. Matthew 20:13.
WRONG, adverb Not rightly; amiss; morally ill; erroneously.
WRONG, verb transitive
1. To injure; to treat with injustice; to deprive of some right, or to withhold some act of justice from.
2. To do injustice to by imputation; to impute evil unjustly.
scriptures: Matthew 20:13
But he answered one of them and said, Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius?
Colossians 3:25
But he who does wrong will be repaid for what he has done, and there is no partiality.
corruption_summary: Wrong is corrupted when 'my truth' dissolves the line, when envy is baptized as a justice claim, and when injury is treated as the same thing as a verdict from God.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the sovereign self. Webster still knew wrong as deviation from a line God prescribed. The age catechizes children that nothing is wrong except making someone feel wrong. Colossians 3:25 still says the one who does wrong will be repaid.
The second corruption is envy as lawsuit. Matthew 20:13 is the landowner answering the grumble: I am doing you no wrong. You agreed. Resentment at another man's wage is not proof of injustice.
The third corruption is 'wrong side of history' as a substitute for the law of God. History is not the judge. God is. A crowd's later sneer does not rewrite the line.

usage: Name the line God drew; a feeling is not a verdict (Colossians 3:25).
Do not call envy a wrong done to you when you agreed to the wage (Matthew 20:13).
Do not dissolve wrong into 'my truth,' and do not confuse a wound with the law.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints LOSE as verb transitive (to mislay; to forfeit; not to gain; to be deprived of; to waste; to ruin) and as verb intransitive (not to win; to decline). Preterit and participle lost. This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: to be deprived or to waste, and to lose life for Christ's sake. Companion pages already treat life, soul, and world.
biblical_def:
Lose is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. To be deprived; to forfeit; to waste; not to keep. To lose is to part with a thing so as not to know where it is, to forfeit in contest, to suffer waste, to throw away. Salt that has lost its savor is Webster's own biblical example. Loss is real. It is not automatically martyrdom.

2. To lose life and find it. Jesus says, whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it. What profit is it to gain the world and lose the soul. The dictionary therefore keeps lose from becoming a pep-talk. Some losses are judgment. Some are discipleship. The cross decides which.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: LOSE, verb transitive — to mislay; to forfeit; not to gain; to be deprived of; to suffer waste; to ruin; to wander from; to waste; to throw away. LOSE, verb intransitive — not to win; to decline. Preterit and participle lost.
webster_full: LOSE, verb transitive looz. preterit tense and participle passive lost.
1. To mislay; to part or be separated from a thing, so as to have no knowledge of the place where it is.
2. To forfeit by unsuccessful contest; as, to lose money in gaming.
3. Not to gain or win; as, to lose a battle, that is, to be defeated.
4. To be deprived of.
5. To forfeit, as a penalty. Our first parents lost the favor of God by their apostasy.
6. To suffer diminution or waste of. If the salt hath lost its savor, wherewith shall it be salted?
10. To possess no longer; to be deprived of; contrary to keep.
12. To waste; to squander; to throw away.
18. to fail to obtain. He shall in no wise lose his reward.
LOSE, verb intransitive looz.
1. To forfeit any thing in contest; not to win.
2. To decline; to fail.
scriptures: Matthew 16:25
For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.
Matthew 16:26
For what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?
corruption_summary: Lose is corrupted when self-preservation is baptized as wisdom, when losing the soul is treated as a branding risk, and when 'you can't lose' is sold as faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the saved self. Matthew 16:25 is whoever desires to save his life will lose it. The age catechizes men to protect the brand, the brand of me. Jesus calls that the losing.
The second corruption is world-gain as scoreboard. Matthew 16:26 still asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and lose the soul. Career religion treats the soul as a rounding error.

The third corruption is prosperity's 'you can't lose.' Webster knew losing as forfeiture and waste. Faith is not a hedge fund. Some men lose because they gambled. Some lose because they followed Christ. Do not mash those.

usage: Do not save the life Christ tells you to lose (Matthew 16:25).
Do not trade the soul for the world and call it winning (Matthew 16:26).
Do not mash waste with discipleship, and do not call self-preservation faith.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints ACCEPT as verb transitive from Latin accepto / accipio (ad + capio, to take): to take what is offered with a consenting mind; to regard with partiality; to consent to terms; in theology, acceptance with God implies forgiveness of sins and reception into His favor. This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: to receive with favor, and to show partiality. Companion pages already treat grace, forgiveness, and partiality.
biblical_def:
Accept is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. To take what is offered with a consenting mind. To accept is to receive with approbation, not merely to have a thing land in your hands. Webster is careful: a man may receive an offer and still not accept it. Moses blesses Levi, Bless his substance, LORD, and accept the work of his hands.

2. To regard with partiality; to be received into God's favor. It is not good to accept the person of the wicked. Malachi asks whether the LORD will accept a man who offers the blind and the lame. In theology, acceptance with God is forgiveness of sins and reception into His favor — not self-esteem with a halo. The dictionary therefore keeps accept from becoming 'accept yourself.' God accepts in the Beloved. A man does not.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: ACCEPT, verb transitive — to take or receive what is offered with a consenting mind; to regard with partiality; to consent to terms; in theology, acceptance with God implies forgiveness of sins and reception into His favor. Observe the difference between receive and accept.
webster_full: ACCEPT', verb transitive [Latin accepto, from accipio, ad and capio, to take.]
1. To take or receive what is offered, with a consenting mind; to receive with approbation or favor.
Bless, Lord, his substance, and accept the work of his hands. Deuteronomy 33:11.
Observe the difference between receive and accept. He received an appointment or the offer of a commission, but he did not accept it.
2. To regard with partiality; to value or esteem. It is not good to accept the person of the wicked.
In theology, acceptance with God implies forgiveness of sins and reception into his favor.
3. To consent or agree to; to receive as terms of a contract.
4. To understand; to have a particular idea of; to receive in a particular sense.
5. In commerce, to agree or promise to pay, as a bill of exchange.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 33:11
Bless his substance, LORD, And accept the work of his hands; Strike the loins of those who rise against him, And of those who hate him, that they rise not again.
Malachi 1:8

And when you offer the blind as a sacrifice, Is it not evil? And when you offer the lame and sick, Is it not evil? Offer it then to your governor! Would he be pleased with you? Would he accept you favorably? Says the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Accept is corrupted when self-acceptance replaces acceptance with God, when partiality is recast as inclusion, and when leftover offerings are treated as generosity He must receive.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is 'accept yourself.' Webster still knew acceptance with God as forgiveness and reception into favor. The age catechizes the conscience to ratify the self. That is not the gospel. It is a rival priest.

The second corruption is inclusion as partiality. Accepting the person of the wicked is an old sin with a new flag. Malachi 1:8 asks whether God will accept a man who offers what he would not offer a governor.
The third corruption is confusing receive with accept. Churches receive every slogan that lands. They do not have to accept it. Webster's distinction still holds.

usage: Ask God to accept the work of your hands, not the brand of your feelings (Deuteronomy 33:11).
Do not offer God what you would not offer a governor and call it worship (Malachi 1:8).
Do not mash receive with accept, and do not replace His favor with self-acceptance.

etymology: Webster 1828 prints REAP as verb transitive (to cut grain with a sickle; to clear a field; to gather as the fruit of labor or of works, in a good or bad sense) and as verb intransitive (to perform the act of reaping; to receive the fruit of labor). Related to Latin rapio, carpo; English crop. Companion pages already treat harvest, sow, and seed.
biblical_def:
Reap is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. To cut grain; to gather a field. To reap is to cut grain with a sickle, and so to clear a crop. When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not wholly reap the corners. Reaping is work under a law of mercy: leave the gleanings.

2. To receive the fruit of what was sown. Whatsoever a man sows, that he will also reap. Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. The harvest can be corruption or life. The dictionary therefore keeps reap from becoming karma merch or a hustle proverb. God is not mocked. A man does not get wheat from thorns by branding the field.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: REAP, verb transitive — to cut grain with a sickle; to clear of a crop; to gather or obtain as the fruit of labor or of works, in a good or bad sense. REAP, verb intransitive — to perform the act of reaping; to receive the fruit of labor or works.
webster_full: REAP, verb transitive [Latin rapio, carpo; Gr. a sickle, to reap; Eng. crop.]
1. To cut grain with a sickle; as, to reap wheat or rye.
When ye reap the harvest, thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field. Leviticus 19:9.
2. To clear of a crop by reaping; as, to reap a field.
3. To gather; to obtain; to receive as a reward, or as the fruit of labor or of works; in a good or bad sense; as, to reap a benefit from exertions.
He that soweth to the flesh, shall of the flesh reap corruption. Galatians 6:7.
REAP, verb intransitive
1. To perform the act or operation of reaping.
2. To receive the fruit of labor or works.
They that sow in tears, shall reap in joy. Psalms 126:5.
scriptures: Galatians 6:7
Do not be deceived, God is not mocked; for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.
Psalm 126:5
Those who sow in tears Shall reap in joy.
corruption_summary: Reap is corrupted when sowing and reaping is recast as karma or manifestation, when harvest is treated as a grindset trophy, and when mercy at the corners of the field is skipped as inefficiency.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is karma with a Bible font. Galatians 6:7 is God is not mocked — not the universe keeping score, not manifestation, not a vision board. A man reaps what he sows because God judges, not because the cosmos is a vending machine.
The second corruption is grindset harvest. Reaping becomes a personal-brand trophy. Psalm 126:5 is sow in tears, reap in joy — a restoration promise, not a productivity hack.

The third corruption is efficiency against gleaning. Leviticus still forbids wholly reaping the corners. A field stripped to the fence is not faithfulness. It is refusing the poor the share God assigned.
